column14: The most valuable aspect of this experience was learning how to complete a project while navigating various challenges. While it may not have been the most enjoyable part, I believe it was the most important lesson of this journey. I’ve learned that people work and communicate differently from me, and this is something I will undoubtedly encounter in the real world. A highlight of the experience was finding that one person on the team I could relate to—someone with whom I could collaborate effectively and share frustrations. It made the process much more manageable and reinforced the importance of building strong working relationships.
column15: The biggest challenge we faced in this team project was communication and collaboration. Team members struggled to communicate clearly about their skills, the tasks they were working on, and offering constructive feedback and opinions. Moreover, collaboration was hindered by a lack of willingness to compromise, with some members prioritizing their own ideas over the team's collective input. Team members often behaved in roles rather than as active participants, leaving little room for pair-programming or team learning opportunities. This ultimately defeated the purpose of developing soft skills during the voyage."

Lack of a product backlog through our the Voyage. Misguided communications between SM and me in 1:1 conversations. Communication and conflict resolution as a team as a result of doing things I was told would be ok to do. 

Not enough virtual meetings, lack of asynchronous checkin since meetings weren’t possible.
column16:
I’m not sure who we designated to submit this. Our last meeting was a couple weeks ago. Personally I really don’t think that Val deserves a certificate, especially as a developer.

Even Ksenia took on assignments that were never complete because they were blocked by other issues we never had backlog items for. Every time I tried to make a ticket or suggest we do something I was told No by Ksenia as if the team already met and decided the answer. However I was never able to figure out where this decision was actually made. Is it possible the team had secret meetings without me? It actually feels this way. She was supposed to create a function to generate color schemes without AI. This task was assigned to her despite it not being part of the MVP and as she pointed out required others to finish their task in order for her to work on it. I questioned her about this once but was ignored. 

I was asked early on to deploy the application to Netlify. Which I did at https://v49-tier2-team-16.netlify.app

Recently it appears that someone has deployed just our development branch elsewhere. This updated branch does not provide secret key to the OpenAI so the work I did to generate images does not work. I’m unsure why this new deploy was made and also why our main branch is not merged with our development branch. 


I really don’t know how I could have done anything different or better. I know I got a little bit upset at times but I believe I remained professional throughout. 

I would love feedback for improving as it seems I’ve let my team down this time.

column10:
Our project is a database of dinosaurs which we named Dinosaur Search (styled dinosaur search). This project is comprised of three features: a Dinosaur Profiles section with a card for each dinosaur along with the ability to search by name, a Dinosaur Map section which is interactive and allows the user to see where dinosaurs originated from by both continent and individual country, and a Dinosaur Diets section which breaks down the diets of dinosaurs by several eras.

This site is also mobile optimized. For our mobile version, many of the interactive features have either been removed or adapted for a better experience on a smaller screen.

column10: Our app is like a virtual Dino world, where you can explore various types of dinosaurs from different eras and regions. We've curated a collection of fascinating information about these ancient creatures. Step into our virtual Dino world, a realm teeming with the majestic creatures that once ruled the Earth. Powered by meticulous data sourced from the renowned National History Museum, this app offers an immersive experience like no other, inviting you to embark on a thrilling journey of discovery through the depths of time.

column16: At the start of the voyage we were grouped to be a team of six members, but to the third sprint, we were only two members who were ready to face reality to build to the requirements of the web app. Honestly I feel proud of my team mate Arman Jena who goes by the discord username Ajena07, because with his perseverance an commitment, I also felt encouraged to continue with the project. More to that my team mate was open to free topic discussions which has helped me learn to be empathetic and understanding as well as revived my  determination for my career goals. If it would be possible I would be glad to be in a team with Ajena07 in any other voyages in the future. Also I would like to gratefully thank the chingu.io administration for organising such an event that unites developers around the world and has helped me grow my soft skills along side my technical knowledge in software development.

column10: The Dino Studio is an exciting educational app to learn all about dinosaurs! Search our list of dinos, see where in the world they were found, who named them, and read about their habitat, diet, and more. Whether you would like to dive into the latest dinosaur discoveries from around the globe or uncover something new about your favorite prehistoric reptile, Dino Studio is the place to do it!

column14: The best aspect of our team project experience was the synergy among our team members, as we embarked on Chingu Voyage 44. We embraced open communication and mutual support, leveraging each other's unique strengths and skills to create something truly exceptional. One example that stands out is when we faced a complex coding challenge, and our team came together, brainstormed ideas, and collaborated closely to devise a solution that exceeded our initial expectations.
column15: The hardest aspect of our team project was navigating the inevitable challenges that arise during the development process. From technical roadblocks to conflicting ideas, we encountered moments of frustration and uncertainty. However, we embraced these difficulties as opportunities for growth and learning. One particular instance that tested our perseverance was when we encountered a critical bug that seemed insurmountable at first. It required extensive debugging, meticulous problem-solving, and persistent teamwork to identify the root cause and implement a solution.
column16: This experience has been incredibly rewarding. While there were difficult moments, I found that facing challenges head-on allowed me to grow both personally and professionally. Collaborating with my teammates, we tackled complex problems, learned from each other, and created something truly remarkable. I am grateful for the opportunity to be part of such a talented and supportive team. The sense of accomplishment we felt upon overcoming obstacles together was truly fulfilling. :)

column14:
I'd say the project management experience for this voyage.

The other teammates are all full-stack engineers, and it's a professional composition. Yet we must align everyone's availability, measure the team's capability and time limitations, to achieve project goals/tasks under different scales.
column15:
One cultural habit I found that from my Indian teammates is - most of them prefer to share thoughts in the meeting and DM instead of in the discord team channel. They consider that they are more professional if they have no problem with the project. I communicated and spent time in team meetings to respect this culture as much as possible. That is, most of the time I spent was on communication.

This also reminds me that sometimes I still have the mindset that I want to make things perfect for sharing… I don’t have to be perfect for every step. The outcome matters to the project result, but the process and the journey could be more than getting the jobs done.
column16: I think I won’t sign up for the next voyage because I hope that I can devote more time to the FOA’s iteration. 😊

column14:
Kirsten: meeting new devs and learning from them was the best aspect of this team project experience, I learned how I can be more organized from members of my team. I also got a new resource from a member too and its been a cool experience. 

Inna: For me, it was a teamwork. I learned a lot from my teammates. Starting from new technologies I never heard about and ending up with the well-known things I didn't understand before
column15:
Inna: It was to organise the work by ourselves and to keep up doing it. It would be much easier to get the tasks from the person who know what has to be done and when, but exactly this issue gave a new experience of planning the project and seeing all its stages. And working with Git, I am absolute zero at team work at Git. 

Kirsten: Router. React. Pain. As a team early on we decided on React as we were all beginners and the project landed up going down the route of using React in a way that was actually a challenge for me. I had to learn router and it gave me so many errors and it broke my app a lot. I had to read a lot to understand why it was breaking and it was a good learning experience overall though. :) React lost a point though. :) Netlify gained one, for clear documentation though.

column13: Figma as a design tool, Python as a data sculpting tool, HTML5 leveraging Webpack to build SCSS and JS files following a Model View Controller structure.
column14:
- Mikey: "The best aspect of the team project for me was being given a prompt and the opportunity to develop a plan to build a web application with other like-minded individuals."
 
- Gabriela: "The best aspect of the program was to complete a project, gain experience and improve soft skills. We were placed in a team to work with, deadlines, other individuals, and shared goals. Also, I realized quickly that I was learning more from this Voyage than from everything I did until now. At this point, I’m grateful because it has been the best experience I’ve ever had :) Thanks a lot, everyone!"

column14: Working and brainstorming together with a talented and supportive team, getting help by the others when you were stuck on a task, working with people from other parts of the world, improving developer skills in React web development and Tailwind CSS. The team worked extremely well together, shared their expertise and all team members supported each other along the way.
column15: hamdi4!#9701 got a job and Carexo#1638 had his final exams, so both dropped out of the project after sprint 4. It was hard for the rest of the team to accept that they have to create a simpler version of the project than they would have liked. The developers said that they might have reached more with the help of two more contributers. Other challenges: Relearning forgotten coding concepts, working together with people across different timezones and scheduling meetings. One of the product owners (without a lot of development experience) learned a lot about the daily struggles that developers face during a team project (GitHub workflow, APIs, website components).
column16: The team overcame all of the aforementioned challenges together, because they all shared their knowledge and expertise. They approached their tasks as a team, had lots of clear communication, were extremely dedicated to the project and every team member can be extremely proud of the success of the project. They were a fantastic team and it was a pleasure to be the product owner of the team together with StellaRose#4959. I learned a lot about project management (and Jira) from her. This Voyage allowed all team members to grow in the areas of project management, development, collaboration with a team and brought lots of personal development. It was definitely a success for everyone who contributed.

column10: The "Toucan T-Shirts" website is a (mock) commercial website where you can browse and filter the products. You can add your preferred t-shirts to your shopping cart, see the products in the cart, checkout and pay (of course only simulated).
column14: The whole team agrees on this: Working as a team, growing together as a team, gaining experience with the use of Git and GitHub in a team project.
column15: Solving (and preventing) merge conflicts. After a while, I (Daniela Küster) got a pretty good intuition on whether there would be a merge conflict or not and I could lead the other team members through the process of avoiding them before they occurred. That was a major skill gain for me!
column16:
Our vision was to create a commercial t-shirt website where the user can browse the wares and add them to their shopping cart. We reached that MVP (minimum viable product) pretty early and even added more functions to the app, including the possibility to check out and pay. Furthermore, we added filters (a search bar and a dropdown menu) to filter by t-shirt name, price or image. Unfortunately, the search bar and dropdown menu have a bug that we were unable to fix in time. Both features were actually "nice to have" features, so we added a detailed bug report to the "issues" section of the repository.

The whole team is very happy that we achieved and even surpassed our goals for the MVP. =)

So, in general, I consider something a worthwhile experience if I learned something useful from it. I learned very many useful things during the Chingu experience, so I consider it worth doing, and I will recommend it to all the other Flatiron software engineer grads. I’m still a little sad we weren’t able to create a worthwhile application though.

Things I learned: 

•        The difficulties of making an OOP DBbase class that mildly resembles what ActiveRecord provides in rails, while still respecting the issues related to parameterized queries in postgres that avoid SQL injection attacks
•        How to setup a decent express backend mvp structure
•        That storing jwt tokens in localstorage is unsecure
•        A setup for express mvp middleware
•        How to work with timestamps in a lot of ways (this will prove immediately applicable to everything I do in the future), on both the frontend and backend.
•        How to use the JSS library in a very basic way to provide javascript styled components


There were many frustrating things for me doing this. Although I guess the biggest frustration for me was a let down of the initial expectation that we could make a complete solid app that would be much better than something I could just build myself in the same amount of time. But it turned out that it was worse than something I could have built myself, because the delayed communication made it harder to write code.

That said, I think our approach from the beginning was bad. We spent too much time thinking about technologies. Should have started iterating on code early on, and not waited so long. 

I worked really hard on this project. About every other day, after I got home from working with my students (mostly reading now), would write some code. Sometimes though it felt a little like one of those school projects where some students don’t care too much about getting the project done. Although it wasn’t really that way. Noah had a lot of RL stuff going on with work. I think Tess just wanted more direction, but with Michael’s initial JSS setup it was hard to get into. Michael did a lot of work, and it was great. But he just disappeared 10 days ago. Basically, he gave up on the project. I don’t know the reason. I appreciate his contributions, but I don’t like it when someone just gives up on a project. Maybe he had RL stuff going on though, who knows.

I wonder if it would be helpful for Chingu to provide recommendations on project architecture and testing. That might seem out-of-scope, but I think there are industry-standard concepts and practices that everyone ought to become familiar with as soon as they want to work professionally. There could be a baseline Chingu recommendation that teams could modify. This isn't the same as something like OOP design patterns -- I just mean general things like Chingu's recommendations for testing (given the six weeks) and architecture (what does proper separation of concerns between views, application logic, database logic, and controllers look like, and what are the benefits and costs?). Chingu could be a great place (perhaps in Tier 2 or 3) to get people thinking and communicating about these things. It might also make it easier for less-experienced developers to get onboarded onto new technologies that they learn as part of their voyage. I suspect that some members of my team were hesitant to take on some tasks because the both the architecture and the technology were alien to them.

Perhaps other teams had this issue as well.

column13: React.js, backend API hosted on fly.io
column14: As already in my first Chingu voyage, it was fantastic to see how we grew together as a team. This time, the others pushed me towards learning new things and I was surprised that I could probably achieve more with React than I initially thought. I had a tough time during the project and the patience and support of the group made it possible for me to finish the project anyways.
column15: The hardest aspect (for the whole team) was to admit defeat and to see that we as a tier 2 group couldn't pull off a tier 3 project. Most of the members of our team signed up for a tier 2 project, but one of us had signed up for a tier 3 project and was accidentally assigned to our group. We decided to design our project in a way that allows data handling with the backend API coded by team member -N-#8679 so that he doesn't need to change teams and can contribute to the project. Unfortunately, we only managed to connect the log in page to the API to check if the user is logged in correctly (the user name and password are "string"). The sign up page isn't connected to the API yet, the kanban board and the to-do list app work independently from the API. We definitely reached our MVP (making a simple to do list app), but an advanced goal would be to handle the data of all parts with the backend API/database.
column16:
I forgot to add that to the README, but we have another GitHub repository for the backend. It's here: https://github.com/chingu-voyages/v41-geckos-team-14-be

We didn't achieve all the goals that we wanted to achieve. For example, the navigation is a bit clunkier than I would like (no navigation bar, going back and forth in the browser window). My perfectionism would normally kick in here, but I'm *very* proud of what my team achieved in this project under pretty difficult circumstances. I learned a ton of new things about React.js and I can't wait to build my next project with it!

StackCafe matches projects with developers based on tech stack.

We are a MERN-based platform for the sharing and publishing of tech stacks behind projects. Developers can search to find projects that match their tech stack interests and can also apply to join projects as team members.
column14: Learning new node.js and MongoDB technologies. Working on a team to design features of a web application. Opportunity to define the product itself and the variety of technologies used.
